cards.title: What is Git?
body: Git is a tool that runs on your computer and tracks changes to your files. Each time you save a snapshot, Git remembers exactly what your project looked like at that moment. Break something later? Jump back to a snapshot. Think of it like save points in a game.

cards.title: What is GitHub?
body: GitHub is a website that stores your Git projects online. It's where you back up your work, share it, and build things with other people. If Git is your save file, GitHub is the cloud save.

cards.title: How they fit together
body: Git does the tracking on your laptop. GitHub is where you upload it. You can use Git without GitHub, but GitHub is built on top of Git.

bullets: `git help`: lists the most common commands

lessons.title: Setting up Git
lessons.says: I just got a new laptop. Help me set up Git before class!

user.name: Jackson Stark
user.backstory: Jackson just got a new laptop and needs to set up Git before class tomorrow.

cards.title: Installing Git
body: First, Git has to be on your computer. Pick your system:

tabs.label: Windows
tabs.text: Download Git from git-scm.com and run the installer. The default options are fine. It also installs Git Bash, a terminal you can use for Git.

tabs.label: Mac
tabs.text: Open Terminal and type `git --version`. If Git isn't installed, your Mac will offer to install it for you.

tabs.label: Linux
tabs.text: Open a terminal and run `sudo apt install git` (Ubuntu/Debian).

cards.footer: Then check it worked with `git --version`, just like in Lesson 1.

cards.title: Tell Git who you are
body: Every snapshot you save is signed with your name and email, so everyone on a project can see who changed what. It's like a signature, not a login. You only need to set this up once per computer.

cards.title: The setup commands
body: Two commands tell Git who you are:
cards.footer: `--global` means "use this for every project on this computer." Put your name in quotes because it has a space. If it worked, Git prints nothing. In the terminal, no news is good news.

lessons.title: Main commands
lessons.says: I built a weather app. Let's save it with Git so nothing gets lost.

user.name: Charley Dunkel
user.backstory: Charley just built a small weather app for a class project. Now Charley wants to start saving it with Git, so nothing gets lost.

cards.title: Saving in Git takes steps
body: In a game, you hit save once. In Git, saving is a few steps, so you get to choose exactly what goes into each snapshot. Think of it like packing a box: first you put things in, then you seal it and write a label.
cards.diagram: [ Your files ]  --git add-->  [ Ready to save ]  --git commit-->  [ Snapshot saved ]

cards.title: `git init`: turn Git on
body: Git doesn't watch every folder on your computer. You have to turn it on for each project. Run `git init` inside a project folder, and Git starts tracking it. You only do this once per project.

cards.title: `git status`: check what's going on
body: `git status` shows what changed and what's ready to save.
bullets: Red files: changed, but not ready to save yet
cards.footer: It never changes anything, so use it whenever you're unsure.

cards.title: `git add` and `git commit`: pack and seal
bullets: `git add .` puts every change in the folder into the box. The dot means "everything here."
`git commit -m "message"` seals the box and saves the snapshot. The message describes what you changed.

lessons.title: Putting it on GitHub
lessons.says: My portfolio only lives on my laptop. Time to put it on GitHub!

user.name: Lily Lurvey
user.backstory: Lily built a portfolio website and has been saving snapshots with Git. But right now it only lives on Lily's laptop. Time to put it on GitHub so the world can see it.

cards.title: Your saves are only on your laptop
body: Every snapshot you've made so far lives only on your computer. If your laptop breaks, they're gone, and nobody else can see your work. Uploading to GitHub fixes both: it's a backup and a way to share.

cards.title: Get your repo's address
body: First you create an empty repo on the GitHub website. GitHub then gives you its address, a URL. You don't type it out: you copy it. Lily's repo is already created, and the URL is on the profile card with a Copy button.

cards.title: `git remote add`: connect to GitHub
body: `git remote add origin <url>` connects your project to your GitHub repo. `origin` is just a nickname for that GitHub address, so you don't have to type the URL ever again. You only do this once per project.

cards.title: `git push`: upload your snapshots
body: `git push -u origin main` uploads your snapshots to GitHub.
bullets: `origin`: where to send them (your nickname from before)
`main`: which line of snapshots to send (you'll learn more about this in Unit 2)
`-u`: remember this, so next time you can just type `git push`

questions.wrongFeedback: `git push` uploads your snapshots to GitHub. Saving a snapshot is `git commit`.

questions.prompt: In `git remote add origin <url>`, what is `origin`?
options: A nickname for your GitHub repo's address
The name of your first snapshot
questions.wrongFeedback: `origin` is a nickname for the GitHub address, so you don't have to type the URL every time.
